item.title: Dify Status Check: Where Is It Now?
item.author: Unknown
item.description:
Baseline version: GitHub langgenius/dify v1.17.1
Estimated half-life: Quarterly (AI app orchestration and protocol evolution moves fast — keep an eye on plugin and MCP developments)
Nature: Personal research notes, sharing what I found
Motivation: I hadn’t heard much about Dify recently and wondered — did it fall behind, or is it quietly growing somewhere else? So I spent some time digging through public sources and wrote down what I found.

1. A Feeling: Why Does It Seem Like “No One’s Talking About It”?

At least in my own circles, between late 2024 and 2026, I rarely saw anyone discussing Dify. My first reaction was: is it dead?

But after going through the materials, I think this “disappearance” likely comes more from our own shifting attention and Dify’s own strategic pivot:

2023 ~ Mid-2024 (Geek Carnival)                    2025 ~ 2026 (Divergence)
[Individual devs / Prompt engineers]             [Code-first camp (geeks/backend)]
      │                                                │
      ▼                                                ▼
Loved GUI drag-and-drop bots / simple KBs    Shifted to Coding Agents (Cursor/Claude Code)
Dify, FastGPT dominating social media         Shifted to code-native state machines (LangGraph/PydanticAI)
                                               
                                               [Dify's actual pivot]
                                                       │
                                                       ▼
                                           International expansion (Japan / North America / Europe)
                                           Deep enterprise (compliance / private deployment / global giants)

1.1 The Geek World’s Attention Shifted

  • In 2023 to early 2024, the LLM ecosystem was still figuring out “how to connect models to knowledge bases and prompts.” Visual DAG drag-and-drop was the lowest-barrier, most demo-friendly approach;
  • Later, the tech community’s attention clearly shifted toward Coding Agents (Cursor, Claude Code, etc.) and code-first state machine frameworks (LangGraph, PydanticAI, etc.). With code, Git management and unit testing feel more native. People on social media stopped posting “wiring diagrams.”

1.2 Dify’s Own重心 Shifted

  • From public information, the LangGenius team deliberately reduced their domestic geek marketing volume and poured energy into overseas markets and large enterprise customers;
  • The fastest-growing market is overseas (especially Japan and North America). While domestic social media discussion cooled, Dify was holding hundreds-person summits in Japan, joining AWS official channels, and completing private deployments inside multinational enterprise networks.

2. Publicly Available Business Data

Here are the numbers I found from public sources, for reference:

2.1 Funding

  • $30M Series Pre-A (March 2026):

    • Lead: HSG (HongShan);
    • Followers: GL Ventures, 5Y Capital (returning investor), Mizuho Leaguer Investment, Alt-Alpha Capital, and NYX Ventures;
    • Valuation approximately $180M.

2.2 Open Source & Community

  • GitHub Stars: ~158K (global Top 60), 1000+ contributors, 861 recent commits, 168 releases;
  • Global self-hosted installations: Over 1.4 million machines;
  • Enterprise customers: Publicly disclosed 280+, including Maersk, Volvo, Novartis, ThermoFisher;
  • Global presence: Offices in San Francisco Bay Area, Tokyo, Shanghai, and Suzhou;
  • Japan market: Established the “Japan Association for Dify” (一般社团法人 Dify 协会, founded September 2025 with NTT Data and others), and became an AWS Global Partner (awarded 2025 AWS Social Impact Partner of the Year).

3. Product & Technical Evolution (v0.x to v1.17+)

From the version history, Dify’s product form has clearly moved well beyond the early “visual prompt tuner” stage. The underlying tech stack has gone through multiple deep refactors:

                    ┌─────────────────────────────────┐
                    │       Dify Marketplace          │ (Plugin ecosystem / Community assets)
                    └────────────────┬────────────────┘
                                     │
┌───────────────────────────────┐    │    ┌───────────────────────────────┐
│        New Agent App          │    │    │       Workflow Studio         │
│ (Autonomous reasoning /      │◄───┴───►│ (Visual orchestration /       │
│  Skills / Code sandbox)      │         │  Branching / Dynamic routing) │
└───────────────┬───────────────┘         └───────────────┬───────────────┘
                │                                         │
                └───────────────────┬─────────────────────┘
                                    ▼
       ┌────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
       │   MCP Gateway (Workflow-as-MCP-Server / ClientPassthru)│
       └────────────────────────────┬───────────────────────────┘
                                    ▼
       ┌────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
       │     Core Engine (Async non-blocking / Sandbox / RBAC)   │
       └────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

3.1 Full MCP (Model Context Protocol) Support

  • Workflow-as-MCP-Server: Complex business workflows orchestrated inside Dify can be exposed as standard MCP Servers with one click. Whether it’s Claude Desktop, an IDE, or an external Coding Agent, they can all call Dify workflows as standard MCP tools;
  • Runtime dynamic header pass-through: Supports injecting placeholder authentication at request time (e.g., {{request.headers.X-Custom-Auth}}), solving the security isolation and identity authentication challenge for multi-tenant enterprises calling third-party tools.

3.2 Plugin System & Marketplace — Fully Decoupled

  • No more forking source code: In the early v0.x days, community developers wanting to integrate a new model or private internal system often had to fork the repo, modify core code, or even maintain their own version. v1.0 (early 2025) restructured the plugin architecture — tools and models are fully decoupled as independent plugins;
  • Marketplace & plugin security governance: Introduced plugin security levels, signature verification, and sandbox isolation. Enterprise users can deploy private plugin sources on internal networks, balancing extensibility with compliance.

3.3 Agent Architecture Rebuild: New Agent App & Sandbox Execution

  • Chat-driven Agent building: Supports generating and debugging agents through natural language conversation, automatically extracting and distilling structured, reusable Skills;
  • Built-in secure sandbox (DifySandbox): Provides isolated Python/Shell execution sandboxes for Code nodes and Tool nodes, supporting secure data transformation, logic decisions, and local script execution;
  • Bidirectional workflow nesting: You can embed Agent nodes inside Workflows (letting the agent make local autonomous decisions), or have Agents trigger specific Workflows.

3.4 Enterprise Core & Compliance

  • Async non-blocking execution engine: Database writes and long-chain calls are async-ified. Multi-branch parallel execution time is optimized from “simple sum of all branches” to “depends on the longest branch,” significantly reducing timeout interruption rates;
  • Enterprise governance certifications: Two consecutive years of SOC 2 Type II, ISO 27001:2022, and GDPR compliance certifications, with full audit log tracking and fine-grained RBAC permission controls.

4. My Attempt to Understand Its Positioning

Here’s my personal understanding from research — may not be fully accurate, just for reference:

DimensionDify (v1.17+)Code-First Frameworks (LangGraph etc.)Pure SaaS Competitors (Coze)
Audience I observeCross-functional teams (Business + IT)Senior backend, AI full-stack engineersIndividual content creators, non-technical ops
Deployment flexibilityOpen-source community / Container private / Multi-cloudPure code library, deploy as you wishDeeply tied to platform ecosystem
Debugging experienceGood node-level historical I/O inspection UIRelies on code breakpoints, LangSmith, etc.Relies on platform logs
Extension approachPlugin marketplace + MCP + Custom code nodesPure code, unlimited extensionLimited to platform’s integration library
Engineering collaborationWorkflow DSL import/export, weaker Git diffingNative Git + unit testsIn-platform version management

My Personal Scenario Understanding

                    Where does your scenario lean?
                              │
         ┌────────────────────┴────────────────────┐
         ▼                                         ▼
【Business-IT collaboration needed】        【Hardcore geek / Algorithm experiments】
• Need to visually present flows to biz    • Logic heavily depends on complex recursion, dynamic backtracking
• Need out-of-box RAG, permissions & audit • Heavily dependent on Git branching & automated testing
• Need multi-model aggregation & MCP GW    • More comfortable with pure code, averse to UI wiring
         │                                         │
         ▼                                         ▼
   Dify might be a good fit             LangGraph / custom code might be handier

This is just my rough personal understanding. Real-world selection is far more complex. Many teams probably use a mix.

5. Monetization & Team Status

This is what I was curious about: Is it making money? Is the team still alive?

5.1 Pricing (Publicly Available)

PlanPriceNotes
SandboxFree200 message credits/month, 1 person, 5 Apps
Professional$59/mo ($590/yr)5,000 credits/month, 3 people, 50 Apps
Team$159/mo ($1,590/yr)10,000 credits/month, 50 people, 200 Apps
EnterpriseCustom quoteSSO/SCIM, private deployment, SLA
AWS Marketplace EnterpriseFrom $150,000/yrListed on AWS Marketplace at this price
Self-hosted communityFree (open-source)Users pay for infra + LLM API costs

5.2 Revenue: Not Disclosed, but Profitable

Dify is a pre-Series-A company and hasn’t publicly disclosed specific revenue figures. But from a Forbes interview (2026-02-24), one key data point is confirmed:

“The company built around it employs 100 people, is profitable and serves more than 280 enterprise customers.”

— Profitable, 100-person team. Specific revenue unknown.

Rough estimate (purely personal speculation, no public basis):

  • Of 280+ enterprise customers, assuming some go through Enterprise (AWS lists at $150K+/yr), plus Cloud subscription revenue
  • 100-person team + four offices, and already profitable — means revenue covers costs
  • Notably, Dify’s official careers page states “Over 60% of our codebase is built by LLMs” — R&D efficiency is likely far higher than traditional teams

5.3 Layoffs: None Found

In Layoffs.fyi and various tech layoff trackers, no Dify/LangGenius layoff records were found. Against the backdrop of massive tech industry layoffs in 2025-2026, this is a positive signal.

5.4 Hiring: Still Recruiting

Dify’s official careers page (join.dify.ai) as of 2026-09-18 still had 4 open positions:

  • LTS Backend Software Engineer (China)
  • Backend Development Intern (China)
  • UI/UX Designer (China)
  • Developer Relations Intern (Community Operations)

Not a large hiring scale, but shows the team is actively running, not frozen.

5.5 Development Activity: Very Active

From GitHub data:

  • Recent versions: v1.17.1 (2026-09-10), v1.15.0 (2026-06-25), v1.14.2 (2026-05-19) — maintaining at least one release per month
  • Weekly activity: ~615 new Stars, 132 Pushes
  • Issue activity: New Issues still being filed as recently as 2026-10-13, with active Maintainer responses
  • Contributors: 1000+, 23.9K Forks

6. Personal Takeaways

  1. Dify didn’t disappear — it just went somewhere I can’t easily see: From the domestic geek community’s perspective, it’s certainly gone “quiet.” But from the overseas enterprise market, Japan ecosystem, and AWS channels, it seems to be running fast on a different track;
  2. Low-code orchestration probably still has its place in enterprise scenarios: While Code-First is the geek aesthetic mainstream, many real business scenarios need cross-department collaboration, visual auditing, and permission controls — these may not be what pure code frameworks do best;
  3. 100 people, profitable, 60%+ code built by LLMs — this combination is interesting in itself. It might be an early example of AI-native development: using AI to build AI tools, a small team leveraging massive scale;
  4. Missing specific revenue numbers is the biggest gap in this research. Understandable for a pre-Series-A company. But from “profitable” and the $150K/yr AWS Enterprise price tag, the business model seems to be working at least.

All of the above is my personal understanding from research — inevitably with some bias. If you see different information, I’d welcome the correction.

item.title: Browser Automation MCP Decision: chrome-devtools-mcp vs. Obscura
item.author: Unknown
item.description:
When equipping an AI coding agent with browser automation capabilities, developers must balance human-agent collaboration, memory overhead, and bot-detection resilience. This post evaluates Google’s official chrome-devtools-mcp against Obscura, a lightweight headless browser built with Rust and V8.

The Core Verdict

These two tools serve fundamentally different workflows:

  • chrome-devtools-mcp is a visual collaborative workspace: It drives a real desktop Chrome instance. Because a visible desktop window is available, you can observe the agent’s actions in real time and take turns interacting with the browser (e.g., handling complex filtering, approving security dialogs, or passing CAPTCHAs by hand before letting the agent resume). It also reuses existing login sessions from your everyday Chrome profile. The tradeoff is heavy memory consumption (~1.5 GB per instance).
  • Obscura is a silent background batch-runner: A headless runtime built on Rust + V8, stripped of any GUI frontend. It does not open desktop windows and cannot support live co-browsing; however, it has an exceptionally small memory footprint (idle at just 23 MB, 98% lower) and conceals obvious headless indicators like navigator.webdriver. It is ideal for quiet background documentation lookups, data scraping, and basic form automation.

Feature Comparison

Dimensionchrome-devtools-mcp (Official)Obscura (Rust + V8)
CollaborationVisible desktop window: Human and agent can share the browser session turn-by-turnHeadless only: Runs silently in the background without UI handoff
Memory FootprintHeavy (idle ~1450 MB, easily stresses concurrent compiler workloads)Minimal (idle ~23 MB)
Bot DetectionHeadless Chrome exposes obvious flags (webdriver=true, HeadlessChrome in UA)Built-in stealth (masks webdriver, synthesizes consistent fake profile)
Form InteractionsFull support for typing, clicking, navigating, and logging inFull support for typing, clicking, navigating, and logging in
Session InheritanceCan attach to your existing local Chrome profile (reuses logged-in cookies)Isolated sandbox; cannot directly inherit desktop profiles
RecommendationUse when co-browsing, session reuse, or deep DevTools diagnostics are requiredBest for concurrent agents, background docs fetching, and mass crawling

Benchmark Data

Environment: WSL2 / Ubuntu 24.04, target URL: example.com.

1. Memory Usage

StateObscura serveChrome headless
Idle23 MB (1 process)1452 MB (14 processes)
Post Page Load26 MB1561 MB (15 processes)

The 50x–60x gap in memory footprint is real. While running heavy compilation jobs or orchestrating multiple concurrent sub-agents, Chrome headless can quickly starve system RAM.

2. Fingerprinting & Bot Detection

Default headless Chrome leaks two glaring signals:

  • navigator.webdriver === true
  • User-Agent prominently displaying HeadlessChrome

Many websites block incoming traffic based on these two checks alone. When started with --stealth, Obscura resets navigator.webdriver to false and presents a consistent Windows / Chrome 145 fingerprint. Note, however, that getContext('webgl') evaluates to null, which advanced anti-bot systems may still flag.

Setup & Configuration

1. chrome-devtools-mcp

"chrome-devtools": {
  "command": "npx",
  "args": ["-y", "chrome-devtools-mcp@latest"],
  "description": "Chrome DevTools MCP"
}

Defaults to headed mode (visible window). Append --headless if you prefer silent execution. Requires local Chrome.

2. Obscura Setup

# Download and unpack the prebuilt stealth binary into ~/.local/bin
curl -L -o obscura.tar.gz "https://github.com/h4ckf0r0day/obscura/releases/download/v0.2.2/obscura-x86_64-linux-stealth.tar.gz"
tar -xzf obscura.tar.gz
mkdir -p ~/.local/bin && mv obscura obscura-worker ~/.local/bin/
chmod +x ~/.local/bin/obscura ~/.local/bin/obscura-worker

MCP server configuration:

"obscura": {
  "command": "obscura",
  "args": ["mcp", "--stealth", "--allow-private-network"],
  "description": "Obscura lightweight headless browser MCP"
}

Clash TUN Mode Gotcha:
In TUN mode, Clash’s fake-ip resolver maps all domains to 198.18.x.x. This triggers Obscura’s internal SSRF guard and cuts off outbound requests. Passing --allow-private-network is mandatory in such environments to allow normal web access.

item.title: Big Model Radar: An AI-Maintained Dashboard for CLI Tool Ecosystems
item.author: Unknown
item.description:
The AI Coding Agent space moves fast. Claude Code, Codex, Gemini CLI, Qwen Code, and others generate a constant stream of Issues, PRs, and discussions daily. No one can keep up with all of it.

I recently discovered Big Model Radar, a project that uses GitHub Actions to automatically scrape development activity from these tools and generates bilingual (Chinese/English) daily reports using LLMs. It has been producing reports steadily every day since July 7, 2026.

Note: The Web UI is a snapshot of the old version (content up to 2026-05). For the latest reports, check Issues or Telegram.

What It Tracks

7 major CLI tools: Claude Code / OpenAI Codex / Gemini CLI / GitHub Copilot CLI / Kimi Code CLI / OpenCode / Qwen Code.

It generates 5 types of daily reports:

  • digest: Cross-tool community activity comparison
  • hn: Hacker News AI hot topics
  • trending: GitHub AI trending repositories
  • web: Anthropic/OpenAI official site updates
  • openclaw: OpenClaw ecosystem report

More Than Just Summaries

Each tool’s daily report contains 6 sections:

  1. Today’s Overview: A paragraph summarizing the day’s key signals
  2. Releases: New version listings
  3. Top 10 Hot Issues: Each with priority + comment count + significance analysis
  4. Top 7-10 Important PRs: Each with feature description + impact assessment
  5. Feature Request Trends: Directional insights extracted from Issues/PRs
  6. Developer Focus Areas: Pain point clustering + high-frequency demand aggregation

This isn’t simple Issue forwarding. It’s a hybrid of AI-generated summaries + trend analysis.

Three-Stage Pipeline: Production → Bridge → Consumption

The project’s architecture is interesting:

  1. Production: The maintainer pays for LLM tokens. GitHub Actions automatically generates daily reports at 08:00 CST, writing to GitHub Issues + Markdown files
  2. Bridge: The project provides MCP Server source code. Users deploy their own instance to Cloudflare Workers, exposing query APIs (list_reports / get_latest / get_report / search)
  3. Consumption: Users connect their own Claude Desktop to the MCP Server for queries, consuming their own LLM tokens

The essence: producers pay to generate content, consumers pay to query it. The MCP Server is a data bridge that lets AI agents consume Issue data directly, instead of humans browsing pages.

Access Methods

  • Web UI: gsscsd.github.io/big_model_radar
  • GitHub Issues: loxehate.github.io/issues
  • RSS: feed.xml
  • Telegram: t.me/agents_radar
  • MCP Server: Self-deployed to Cloudflare Workers

An Interesting Reality

As of 2026-07-12, there are zero human comments across 41 issues.

Issues in this project serve as persistent storage for AI-generated content, not a discussion forum. All channels are unidirectional — AI generates → humans/AI consume. There is no “human feedback to AI” loop.

An accurate description: AI generates, AI consumes, humans observe.

Value

Reduces information acquisition costs — from “manually checking 7 repositories daily” to “glancing at a daily report”; enables cross-tool comparison; provides trend awareness; AI analysis offers directional insights.

item.title: Enhancing AI Code CLI Capabilities Should Use MCP Protocol, Not Built-in Tool Source Code
item.author: Unknown
item.description:
Don’t build on code that’s about to be deleted.

What Happened

The older version of Qwen Code had a built-in web_search tool supporting three search backends: Tavily, Google, and DashScope (DashScope was eligible for Qwen OAuth authentication). But its provider selection was static — you’d configure a single default, the tool would call that one provider per search, and failures were just errors. No fallback.

My goal was to add runtime provider fallback inside the tool: try Tavily first, then Google, then DashScope. If the first one fails, automatically move to the next. That way a single backend going down wouldn’t kill search entirely.

On 2026-04-24, while my solution was still local — Qwen Code PR #3502 landed. It deleted the entire web_search built-in tool and replaced it with an MCP-based architecture. All the old config keys (webSearch block, advanced.tavilyApiKey, --tavily-api-key CLI flag, etc.) were deprecated. I had been working against a target that no longer existed.

Why This Approach Was Doomed

The problem wasn’t the idea — the old implementation genuinely lacked runtime fallback, and adding it was a reasonable improvement. The problem was the foundation:

  • web_search went from existence to deletion in a single PR. The AI Code CLI category is less than two years old. Built-in tools can be refactored, merged, or deleted at any time.
  • MCP is a cross-CLI standard. Qwen Code, Claude Code, Gemini CLI all support it. Tools built on MCP are independent of any CLI implementation — there’s no risk of “I spent weeks modifying source code, and then the tool got deleted.”

Reflection: The Right Approach

Fallback itself was a good idea — the old version needed it, and the MCP layer needs it too. The mistake was where I chose to implement it:

  • ❌ Modifying CLI built-in tool source code to add fallback
  • ✅ Writing a standalone MCP server that internally handles multi-provider fallback

Same functionality. Placed in built-in tool source, it’s one PR away from deletion. Placed in an MCP server, it’s decoupled from the CLI version lifecycle — you control when it lives or dies.

Takeaways

  • When building capability enhancements for AI Code CLIs, prioritize the MCP layer — tools live independently of CLI implementation, immune to upstream refactoring.
  • Before you start, check the module’s lifecycle: is it stable core functionality, or experimental code that could be replaced at any time?

item.title: Getting Qwen Code to Work with Tavily Search
item.author: Unknown
item.description:
1. Get an API Key

Sign up at Tavily and copy your API key.

2. Set the Environment Variable

Persist TAVILY_API_KEY as a system environment variable (replace tvly-xxxxxxxx with your actual key).

Linux / macOS:

echo 'export TAVILY_API_KEY="tvly-xxxxxxxx"' >> ~/.profile
source ~/.profile

If you’ve already set this before, open ~/.profile in an editor to replace or remove the old entry — avoid duplicate lines.

Windows (PowerShell):

[Environment]::SetEnvironmentVariable("TAVILY_API_KEY", "tvly-xxxxxxxx", "User")

No admin privileges required. This writes a persistent environment variable for the current user, but doesn’t modify the already-open PowerShell process — close and reopen the terminal for it to take effect.

After reopening PowerShell, verify:

$env:TAVILY_API_KEY

If you want to continue testing immediately in the current PowerShell window without reopening, sync it once:

$env:TAVILY_API_KEY = [Environment]::GetEnvironmentVariable("TAVILY_API_KEY", "User")

Your API key grants access to a paid tier. Run the commands above yourself — don’t let an AI agent do it for you.

3. Install Tavily MCP

Tell Qwen Code:

Please install Tavily MCP using the qwen mcp add command, then search for something to verify it works.

Done.

Verified: 2026-05-05, Qwen Code 0.15.6 + tavily-mcp 0.2.19
